options: A single installable operating system identical across every vendor
A kernel that different distributions package with their own tools and configuration
A graphical desktop environment
A brand name for Red Hat's product line only
questions.explain: Linux is the kernel. Distributions like Ubuntu, Debian, and Red Hat Enterprise Linux each package that same kernel family with their own userland tools, package manager, and configuration.

questions.q: Where do core command-line tools like ls, cp, and grep actually come from?
options: The Linux kernel source tree itself
The GNU Project, paired with the kernel to form a complete system
Microsoft's open-source contributions
Each distribution writes its own from scratch
questions.explain: The GNU Project supplies most of the core userland utilities. The Linux kernel plus GNU tools together form what's commonly just called "Linux."

questions.q: Which command tells you the distribution name and version you're logged into?
options: uname -a
cat /etc/os-release
ps aux
df -h
questions.explain: /etc/os-release is the standard plain-text file nearly every modern distribution maintains with its name, ID, and version. uname -a reports kernel version and architecture instead.

questions.q: Why are Docker containers described as a Linux-native idea?
options: Because containers bundle their own full copy of the Linux kernel
Because containers rely directly on Linux kernel features — namespaces and cgroups — rather than carrying their own kernel
Because Docker only runs on Linux desktops, never servers
Because containers were invented by the GNU Project
questions.explain: A container isolates processes using the host kernel's namespaces and limits resources using cgroups. It borrows the host's kernel rather than shipping its own, which is why containers originated on Linux.

questions.q: Which of these is a genuine, practical reason DevOps tooling defaults to assuming Linux?
options: Linux cannot run any graphical software
Most cloud VMs run Linux and it carries no per-core licensing cost at scale, and automation tools like Ansible and Terraform assume a Linux shell
Windows Server cannot run in the cloud at all
Linux requires a GUI for all configuration changes
questions.explain: The majority of cloud infrastructure runs Linux partly because it avoids per-core commercial licensing costs, and major automation tools are built around a Linux shell and plain-text configuration.
